title: Friendship: A Bible Study on the Love We Forgot
subtitle: A five-session study on friendship, loneliness, and the covenant of companions.
summary:
This study is for anyone who has more contacts than ever and fewer friends than they'd like to admit, and for the small groups willing to say so out loud. It moves slowly through five sessions: the love the modern world quietly demoted, and the loneliness that followed; the covenant of David and Jonathan, who bound their souls together in a court that wanted one of them dead; the friend who wounds faithfully when a flatterer would have kept the peace; the strange thing Jesus said the night before he died, when he called his followers friends; and the ordinary work of keeping a friendship alive in a mobile, distracted, tired age. A busy volunteer can lead it with little preparation. Every question carries notes on what's behind it, and every session ends in prayer.

It doesn't stand above friendship handing out advice. Most of us have let a friendship starve because we were busy, kept the acquaintance and lost the brother, and confused being surrounded with being known, and the study begins there, with the writer and the leader included. Nor will it pretend friendship is a small thing you get to once the important loves are handled. Scripture calls it a love strong enough to knit two souls, faithful enough to wound, and costly enough that the Son of God gave his life for his friends and then called us that. We forgot it was a love at all. This study is an attempt to remember.
audience: Anyone carrying loneliness, and the small groups that meet honestly

sessions.title: The Love We Stopped Naming
sessions.aim: To recover friendship as a real and serious love rather than a lesser bond you get to once the important relationships are handled, and to see the loneliness of our time not only as a private failure but as the predictable fruit of a world that quietly demoted the very love it now aches for.
sessions.summary:
Ask people whom they'd call if they landed in the hospital, and many aren't sure. Then they add quickly that they're fine, that they have plenty of people. That's a life full of contacts and short of friends, and it isn't rare. C. S. Lewis observed in The Four Loves (1960) that the ancients ranked friendship among the highest human goods and the modern world largely ignores it. Aristotle had long before sorted friendship into three kinds: the friendship of usefulness, the friendship of pleasure, and the rare, slow friendship of two people who want each other's good, which is the only kind that lasts.

There's a strong case for how we live now. Adults are busy, family and work rightly come first, and friendship can look like a luxury for people with time. Some of that is true. But in 2023 the U.S. Surgeon General issued an advisory calling loneliness an epidemic, and Scripture said long ago that it isn't good for a human being to be alone. We didn't lose friendship to bad luck. We traded it, one reasonable postponement at a time, and we're only now counting the cost.

keyScripture.why: "Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their toil. For if they fall, one will lift up his fellow. But woe to him who is alone when he falls and has not another to lift him up!" (Ecclesiastes 4:9-10). The Preacher treats companionship as a basic human need, not a luxury for people with time, and being alone when you fall as a real danger, not a badge of strength.

discussion.q: Think of the person with plenty of contacts who doesn't know whom he'd call from a hospital bed. Is that closer to your life than you'd like to admit? How did it get that way?
discussion.behind: Start with an inventory before any theology. Most people have quietly accepted a life of acquaintance and would rather not name it. You aren't trying to pull a confession of loneliness out of anyone. You're letting the gap between how connected we look and how known we are come into the open. Naming it is the first work; don't rush to a fix.

discussion.q: Aristotle said most friendships are kept because they're useful or because they're fun, and only a few because two people truly want the good for each other. Look at your own friendships. Which kind are most of them, and does that surprise you?
discussion.behind: Give people a real tool and let them use it on themselves. Friendships of usefulness and pleasure aren't sins; they're normal and even good. But a life made only of them is thinner than it looks, because both dissolve when the usefulness or the fun runs out. Let the room notice how few of the third kind they have, and let that sit.

discussion.q: Lewis said the modern world largely ignores the love the ancients ranked near the top. Why do you think we demoted friendship, and what did we tell ourselves we were gaining?
discussion.behind: Move gently from the personal to the cultural. Nobody decided to abandon friendship. We chose mobility, careers, the private household and the convenience of the screen, each for a real good, and friendship was the cost nobody itemized. Help the room see that their loneliness isn't only a personal failure but partly the fruit of an arrangement they were handed.

discussion.q: The Surgeon General compared the health effects of loneliness to smoking. Does it help or bother you to hear it put that plainly, and what does it say that a doctor said it before many churches did?
discussion.behind: This is where the secular finding is brought under Scripture. The research names a real wound, and it's worth grieving that the culture measured the loneliness before the church addressed it. But keep the focus on Scripture, which said it first and said it more deeply: it isn't good for the human to be alone.

discussion.q: Where have you traded a friendship for something that seemed reasonable at the time, and what did you tell yourself?
discussion.behind: Move to self-examination, and go first if the room is slow. The point isn't to hunt for guilt but to see that our loneliness has a history each of us helped write: the call not returned, the friend we let drift, the gathering we skipped because we were tired. Name your own before you ask for theirs.

objections.objection: I'm not lonely. I'm an adult with responsibilities. Friendship is fine for people with free time, but between work and family there's nothing left, and acting as if everyone needs a circle of close friends is romanticizing something optional.
objections.response: There's real truth here. Adult life is full, and the seasons of small children and demanding work are hard on the calendar. No one should be shamed for a thin stretch of years when getting through takes everything, and demanding that a worn-out person manufacture deep friendship on top of it can be its own cruelty. But the objection treats friendship as an extra, a hobby for people with margin, when Scripture treats it as a need as basic as the one God named in the garden: "It is not good that the man should be alone" (Genesis 2:18). The busyness is real, and very often it's also the cover, the respectable name for a slow withdrawal from being known. The person who can't say whom he'd call didn't get there by accident. He got there one reasonable postponement at a time.

objections.objection: I have plenty of friends. I talk to people all day, I have hundreds of connections online, and I never feel isolated. This loneliness talk is overblown, at least for people who put themselves out there.
objections.response: Take that seriously, because being around people is real and social energy is a gift. Some people are richly connected and shouldn't be talked into a crisis they don't have. But there's a difference between company and friendship, and our age makes them easy to confuse. Being surrounded isn't the same as being known. The friendship of pleasure is good and also evaporates when the fun stops, and a feed full of connections can leave a person entirely unknown. The test isn't whether you feel isolated at a party. It's whether there's someone who could tell you a hard true thing, someone you'd call in the worst hour, someone who has seen you at your least useful and stayed. If there is, thank God. If the truthful answer is thinner than the number suggests, the problem isn't overblown. It's well disguised.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: Who is the friend you've let slowly become an acquaintance, and what reasonable-sounding excuse have you used to let it happen?
sessions.practice: This week, take one friendship you've let thin into mere contact and do the inefficient thing. Don't text. Call, or better, visit, with no agenda and nothing to gain. Don't announce it as an experiment. Then, privately, write the list this session asks about, the people you'd actually call from a hospital bed, and sit with what its length tells you. Write down what rises in you when you reach toward someone with no use in mind.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, in the garden you looked at a man who had everything and said it wasn't good for him to be alone, and we've built a world that forgot you said it. We're surrounded and unknown, full of contacts and short of friends, and we've called our loneliness busyness and our withdrawal maturity. Forgive the friendships we traded for convenience and never grieved. Teach us to want another person's good more than their usefulness, and to build the slow kind of love the ancients honored and we ignored. Give us courage to reach toward someone with nothing to gain. In your mercy, give us the friend we'd call in the worst hour, and make us that friend for someone else. Amen.
reflection: How much of my life is contact and how much is friendship, and which have I been mistaking for the other?
Which of Aristotle's three kinds describes most of my friendships, and what would it cost me to build even one of the rare kind?
Where have I called my withdrawal from people maturity or busyness when it was really a slow trading away of a love I now miss?
sessions.teaching:
Ask people whom they'd actually call if they landed in the hospital, and many can't come up with a name they're sure of. Then they add, quickly, that they're fine, that they have plenty of people. Both things are true. They have plenty of people and not one they're sure of, a life full of contacts and short of friends, and it matters because this isn't the exception. It's the shape of our time. So I don't want to start with a technique for making friends. I want to start with a harder question: why did a whole civilization stop treating friendship as a love worth building a life around, and only notice once loneliness had become a public health concern?

C. S. Lewis saw it coming. In The Four Loves, published in 1960, he wrote that friendship is in one sense the least natural of the loves, the least instinctive and biological, and that while the ancients counted it among the happiest and most fully human goods, the modern world largely ignores it. The ancients weren't sentimental about it either. More than three centuries before Christ, Aristotle gave two books of his Nicomachean Ethics to friendship and sorted it into three kinds. There's the friendship of usefulness, kept because the other person can do something for you. There's the friendship of pleasure, kept because the other person is good company. Both are real and neither is evil, but both last exactly as long as the usefulness or the pleasure lasts, because what you loved was what the person gave you. And there's the third kind, the friendship of two people who want each other's good and are made better by knowing each other, who'd still be friends when the usefulness ran dry and the fun went quiet. That kind lasts, Aristotle said, because it rests on the person. It's also rare, because it's slow, and we live in a world with little patience for slow.

There's a strong case for how we live now, and thoughtful people make it. Adults are busy. Family rightly comes first, work is demanding, and the years of raising children and building a career leave almost nothing over. On this view friendship is a luxury for people with margin, something you get to later if you get to it at all. Much of that is true. The busyness isn't imaginary, and the years without margin are hard. But look at what the arrangement is producing. In 2023 the Surgeon General of the United States issued an advisory titled Our Epidemic of Loneliness and Isolation, and it compared the risk to health with that of smoking. It took a doctor to say what Genesis said at the beginning, before anything had gone wrong: "It is not good that the man should be alone" (Genesis 2:18). The church held that word the whole time and largely let the culture discover it first.

Here's where I have to stand inside it. Most of us have let friendships die because we were busy and told ourselves they'd keep. We've kept the acquaintance and lost the brother. We've been surrounded and unknown and called it independence. So when I say we didn't lose friendship to bad luck, I mean all of us. We traded it, one reasonable postponement at a time, for convenience and mobility and the thin company of a screen that asks nothing and gives little back. Scripture had already drawn the line we've lost: "A man of many companions may come to ruin, but there is a friend who sticks closer than a brother" (Proverbs 18:24). Many companions, and one friend who stays. The loneliness of our age isn't a mystery, and it isn't merely a private failure. It's the bill coming due for a world that quietly decided the oldest human need was optional.

scriptureStudy.note: "It is not good that the man should be alone." In a world God keeps calling good, he names one thing not good, and he names it before the fall. Needing another person isn't a weakness brought in by sin. It's part of what a human being is.

"Two are better than one... For if they fall, one will lift up his fellow." The Preacher, who has tried everything and found most of it empty, lands on companionship as a plain good and names the danger of the solitary life: no one to lift you when you fall.
"A threefold cord is not quickly broken." Companionship is strength as well as comfort, the difference between what snaps under strain alone and what holds because it's bound together.

"A man of many companions may come to ruin, but there is a friend who sticks closer than a brother." Scripture itself separates the crowd of companions from the true friend, the distinction our age has lost.
"Do not forsake your friend and your father's friend." Friendship is meant to endure across time and even across generations, a bond to keep rather than a convenience to drop.
"The soul of Jonathan was knit to the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul." Scripture can describe friendship as souls knit together, a love weighty enough to fill the next session.
"But I have called you friends." Jesus reaches for this word at the most solemn moment of his life. If he ranks it that high, our demotion of it isn't neutral.

sessions.goingDeeper:
Look into the history this session only points at, because the West didn't always rank friendship where we do. For the ancients it was among the highest human goods. Aristotle gave it two books of the Nicomachean Ethics, and Cicero wrote his Laelius, On Friendship near the end of his life. A group can weigh what changed. The romantic ideal gradually made marriage the one relationship expected to carry every human need, so friendship came to look like a supporting role. The industrial and then digital reorganization of life scattered people across cities and screens, and the ordinary nearness friendship needs, the neighbor, the parish, the trade, the settled town, thinned out.

Set this beside Robert Putnam's Bowling Alone (2000), which traced the decline across the second half of the twentieth century of the clubs, leagues and civic groups that once wove Americans together, and notice that the loneliness now measured as a health concern has a documented social history. Then take the harder turn underneath it. A culture that made the self-choosing individual its highest value was always going to find friendship difficult, because real friendship binds you, obligates you, and asks you to be inconvenienced by another person's life. Mobility, choice and freedom are real goods, and the aim isn't to despise them. It's to see clearly what they were bought with, and to ask whether anyone meant to pay that price.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose a woman in your group is warm, capable and well liked, the one everyone counts on, who organizes, remembers birthdays and brings meals. When the conversation turns from being useful to being known, she goes quiet, then says almost in passing that she isn't sure anyone knows her the way she knows them. She's always the one giving and rarely the one seen.

Her giving is real and good and too rarely thanked, and you should say so plainly. But she has also just described a life built on being useful, the friendship of usefulness run in the generous direction, and it has left her surrounded and unknown. The giving may have become a way to be needed without the risk of being known. How would you honor what she gives and still ask her, gently, whether she has a friend she lets carry her, or only friends she carries? What would it look like for this group to be a place where she's allowed to receive?

memoryVerse.text: Then the LORD God said, "It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him a helper fit for him."

sessions.title: Souls Knit Together: The Covenant of David and Jonathan
sessions.aim: To see in David and Jonathan a friendship that rises to covenant, sworn, costly and self-giving, and to recover the idea that friendship can be a bond you promise and not only a mood you enjoy, refusing both the sentimentality that makes it a feeling and the cynicism that makes it a transaction.
sessions.summary:
The most striking friendship in Scripture isn't striking for its warmth but for its cost. Jonathan was the crown prince of Israel, and David was the man God had chosen to take the throne, and Jonathan loved him anyway. "The soul of Jonathan was knit to the soul of David," the text says, and then it uses a word we rarely use for friends: covenant. Jonathan made a covenant with David and gave him his robe, the robe of the heir, handing over the future the friendship should have made him fight for.

It wasn't a friendship of usefulness, since David could only cost Jonathan a throne, and it wasn't a friendship of pleasure, since it was forged while Jonathan's father hunted David to kill him. It was a friendship that bound itself by an oath in the name of the LORD, and the binding is what let it hold. There's a real case for keeping friendship light and free. But when Jonathan died, David sang that his love had been "extraordinary, surpassing the love of women," and we've largely lost the category that line assumes: a friendship worth weeping over.

keyScripture.why: "Then Jonathan made a covenant with David, because he loved him as his own soul" (1 Samuel 18:3). The deepest friendship in Scripture is described as a covenant, a bond sworn and sealed rather than only felt, a friendship that chose to bind itself by promise.

discussion.q: Jonathan was heir to the throne, David was chosen to take it, and Jonathan loved him anyway and even helped him. What astonishes you about a friendship where one person gives up his own future for the other?
discussion.behind: Open on the cost before any theology. Most friendships are never tested by whether they'd survive the friend gaining an advantage over us. Jonathan's was, and he chose David over his crown. Let the room feel how rare that is before anyone explains it.

discussion.q: Read 1 Samuel 18:1-4. The text says Jonathan's soul was knit to David's, then calls their bond a covenant. What changes when you think of a friendship as something you could promise and not only something you feel?
discussion.behind: Press on the shift. We keep promises for marriage and blood and treat friendship as a mood that lasts while it lasts. Scripture puts a friendship under oath. Ask whether the lightness we prize in friendship is also what makes it so easy to let die, and what it might mean to commit to a friend, faithfully and not romantically.

discussion.q: Some say friendship is precious precisely because it's free and unbound, something you can walk away from, unlike marriage or family. What's true in that, and what does the freedom cost us?
discussion.behind: Hold both halves. There's real good in friendship being chosen rather than assigned. But the same lack of binding is why friendship is the first thing to go when life gets busy; it's the relationship with no vow to hold it.

discussion.q: Read 1 Samuel 23:15-18. While Saul hunted David, Jonathan went to him and "strengthened his hand in God." What does it look like for a friend to strengthen your hand in God rather than just cheer you up? Who has done that for you?
discussion.behind: Move to the concrete. Jonathan didn't merely comfort David; he pointed him back to God in the worst hour, at risk to himself. Help the room name the difference between a friend who distracts you from the pit and one who meets you in it and points you up.

discussion.q: David said Jonathan's love was "extraordinary, surpassing the love of women," and many readers have been uneasy with that line. Have we lost the ability to love a friend that deeply? What did we lose it to?
discussion.behind: Close on the loss and on ourselves. The unease often says more about us than about David, a culture that can read deep love only as romance. Help the room mourn a category we misplaced, and go first by naming a friendship you let thin that could have been deeper.

objections.objection: This story is being read too intensely. David and Jonathan were allies in a dangerous political situation, and calling it a covenant of the soul projects modern ideas of deep friendship onto what was really a strategic alliance.
objections.response: The caution is fair. Reading our longings into an ancient text is a real danger, and the politics were deadly and real; Jonathan and David were caught in a lethal succession crisis, and that shouldn't be flattened. But the text won't let the bond shrink to strategy, because a strategic alliance runs on advantage, and everything Jonathan does runs against his own. An heir doesn't strengthen the hand of the man who will take his throne, warn him against his own father, or hand him the royal robe, unless something other than advantage is at work. Scripture names it plainly and more than once: a soul knit to a soul, a covenant sworn before God, a love Jonathan chose at the cost of his crown. You don't have to romanticize it to take it seriously. You only have to notice that no calculation of interest explains what Jonathan did.

objections.objection: Making friendship a covenant sounds suffocating. The beauty of friendship is that it's free, with no obligations, and turning it into a sworn commitment would make it one more duty.
objections.response: That fear is guarding something worth protecting. Friendship shouldn't become one more contract to manage, and a version of this that turned friends into obligations would drain the freedom that makes friendship a gift. But look at what the covenant does in the story. It doesn't smother the friendship; it saves it. Because Jonathan and David are bound by oath, the friendship survives Saul's spear, the years of exile and the politics that should have made them enemies. A bond with no strings also has nothing to hold it under strain, which is why so many unbound friendships fade under nothing more dramatic than busyness. Covenant here isn't a cage. It's a chosen faithfulness that says, "I won't let this drift."

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: Is there a single friend you'd give up an advantage for, the way Jonathan gave up a throne? If the answer is no, what does that tell you about how you've loved your friends?
sessions.practice: This week, do one Jonathan thing: one act of friendship that costs you something and gains you nothing, where a friend's good and your own advantage actually compete. And find one friend and, without making it strange, tell them plainly that you're committed to them and won't let the friendship drift. That's the closest thing to Jonathan's covenant most of us can offer. Write down what it stirs in you to love a friend at a cost, and whether you've kept your friendships too light ever to be tested.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord, you gave David a friend who loved him enough to give up a throne, who bound his soul to another and sealed it with an oath in your name, and who went to him in the wilderness and strengthened his hand in you. We've loved our friends more lightly than that, kept them unbound so we could keep them convenient, and let the deep ones drift for want of a promise. Forgive us. Teach us to want a friend's good above our own advantage, to be faithful where we've only been fond, and to strengthen a friend's hand in you rather than merely cheer them up. Give us, and make us, the friend who stays when the spears fly. Amen.
reflection: Have I ever loved a friend at real cost to myself, or have I kept my friendships where they never ask anything of me?
What would it mean to make a covenant of faithfulness with a friend, not a romance and not a contract, but a promise not to let it drift?
Who has strengthened my hand in God in a hard season, and whose hand am I strengthening now?
sessions.teaching:
The most striking friendship in the Bible isn't striking for how warm it was but for how much it cost, and to feel the cost you have to keep the whole situation in view. Jonathan was the crown prince of Israel, son of King Saul and natural heir to the throne. David was the shepherd God had chosen to take that throne instead, a man whose very existence threatened everything Jonathan stood to inherit. Every rule of self-interest said they should be rivals. Saul understood it perfectly. He told Jonathan, "For as long as the son of Jesse lives on the earth, neither you nor your kingdom shall be established" (1 Samuel 20:31), and more than once he hurled a spear at David.

Into that, the text drops a sentence that should stop us: "the soul of Jonathan was knit to the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul" (1 Samuel 18:1). Then it does something we almost never do with friendship: it reaches for covenant. "Then Jonathan made a covenant with David, because he loved him as his own soul. And Jonathan stripped himself of the robe that was on him and gave it to David, and his armor, and even his sword and his bow and his belt" (1 Samuel 18:3-4). That isn't a sentimental gesture. The heir's robe and weapons are signs of his place, and Jonathan gives them to the man who'll sit on the throne in his stead. He's handing over his future.

So what kind of love is this? It isn't the friendship of usefulness, because David can do nothing for Jonathan except take his crown. It isn't the friendship of pleasure, because it's forged in a court where the friend's father is trying to kill the friend. It's the third kind, the love that wants the other's good, and it has risen into covenant, sworn in the LORD's name. "Go in peace, because we have sworn both of us in the name of the LORD, saying, 'The LORD shall be between me and you, and between my offspring and your offspring, forever'" (1 Samuel 20:42).

There's a strong case for keeping friendship lighter than that, and thoughtful people make it. Promises belong to marriage and to blood, the argument goes. The glory of friendship is that it's free, chosen fresh each day, and you can always walk away, and that freedom is what makes it a gift rather than a duty. There's something true there, and I don't want to lose it. But watch what the covenant does in the story. It doesn't cage the friendship; it saves it. Because Jonathan and David are bound by oath, the bond survives the spear, the years of David's exile, and the whole logic of succession that should have made them enemies. When David is hunted in the wilderness of Ziph, "Jonathan, Saul's son, rose and went to David at Horesh, and strengthened his hand in God" (1 Samuel 23:16). He doesn't send encouragement from a safe distance. He goes into the wilderness where the hunted man is hiding, at risk to his own life, and he doesn't merely comfort David. He points him back to God and won't let his friend despair.

Most of us love our friends more lightly than Jonathan loved David, and we know why. Loving lightly is safe. A friendship you keep unbound can never really cost you, never test you, never ask you to cross into anyone's wilderness. Many of us keep our friendships where they ask nothing, call it respecting the other person's freedom, and are really protecting our own.

Then there's the ending, which many readers haven't known what to do with. When Jonathan was killed in battle, David sang a lament: "I am distressed for you, my brother Jonathan; very pleasant have you been to me; your love to me was extraordinary, surpassing the love of women" (2 Samuel 1:26). Some readers today take that line as evidence of a romantic relationship. The text itself frames the bond as covenant friendship sworn before the LORD, and that's how this study reads it. But notice why the line unsettles us. We have one category for love that deep, and it's romance, so we assume the verse must be about that or must be exaggerating. The harder truth is that we've lost the category Scripture assumed, a friendship worth weeping over, a companion love so weighty a king would mourn it in the language of the greatest loves he knew. David wasn't confused about what kind of love it was. We are.

scriptureStudy.note: "The soul of Jonathan was knit to the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul." Friendship described as souls bound together, a weight of love we now reserve for romance.
Jonathan makes a covenant with David and gives him his robe, armor, sword, bow and belt. The heir hands the signs of his place to the man who will take it.
Jonathan tells David, "Saul my father seeks to kill you." Friendship here means siding with the friend even against his own father and his own claim to the throne.

Jonathan makes a covenant with the house of David "and Jonathan made David swear again by his love for him, for he loved him as he loved his own soul." The bond is extended to their descendants, built to outlast them both.
Jonathan "rose and went to David at Horesh, and strengthened his hand in God." The truest work of a friend isn't distraction but entering the pit and pointing the friend back to God.
"We have sworn both of us in the name of the LORD, saying, 'The LORD shall be between me and you.'" The friendship is a bond of three: the two friends and the LORD who witnessed it.

"Your love to me was extraordinary, surpassing the love of women." David grieves a friend in the language of the deepest loves he knows, and our unease at the line shows how small our idea of friendship has become.

sessions.goingDeeper:
Look at how the Christian tradition once thought about deep friendship, because the church has resources here it has mostly forgotten. In the twelfth century Aelred of Rievaulx, a Cistercian abbot, wrote Spiritual Friendship, taking up Cicero's work on the subject and bringing it inside the life of the church. He argued that the truest friendship isn't a distraction from the love of God but a school for it. He even considered whether one might say "God is friendship," as John says "God is love," and while he granted that Scripture doesn't say it, he held that whoever abides in true friendship abides in God. That's a far higher account of friendship than our culture's, and higher than much of the modern church's.

The tradition also carried a caution: friendship can become exclusive, a closed circle of two that shuts others out or loves the friend more than God. It held both, the exalted good and the danger of idolizing it. Then come back to David and Jonathan and the unease their story provokes. Our instinct is either to read any intense love between two men as romance or to flatten it into a political alliance, and either way we show that we've lost the middle category the ancients and medieval Christians kept: a love between friends that is neither romance nor transaction but its own honorable thing. Wesley Hill's Spiritual Friendship is one recent attempt to recover covenant friendship, deliberate, faithful and chaste, as something the church could offer a lonely age. Ask what it would cost us to take friendship that seriously again.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose a man in your group speaks warmly about his friends, but when the covenant theme comes up he gets a little defensive. He says he doesn't really do "the deep, intense thing." He keeps his friendships easy and low-maintenance, and that suits him fine. He isn't cold, and he clearly has people he likes and does things with.

Easy friendships are real and good, and no one is obliged to turn every friendship into a covenant, so don't treat his preference as a defect. But low-maintenance can quietly mean he has arranged his friendships so that none of them can ever cost him anything, so that he never has to cross into anyone's wilderness or be known past the surface. How would you honor his preference and still ask him, gently, whether there's a single friend he'd let his life be inconvenienced for? How would you help him tell the difference between ease and keeping everyone at a safe distance?

sessions.title: Faithful Are the Wounds of a Friend
sessions.aim: To recover the friend who tells the hard truth as an act of love rather than a breach of it, to see truthfulness and accountability as part of real friendship, and to refuse both the false peace that calls flattery kindness and the harshness that calls cruelty honesty.
sessions.summary:
One sure sign that you don't have a close friend is that no one has told you a hard truth about yourself in years. Proverbs puts it more bluntly than we're used to: "Faithful are the wounds of a friend; profuse are the kisses of an enemy." We treat the person who only affirms us as the good friend and the one who challenges us as the difficult one. Scripture says the flatterer is the enemy and the one who wounds you faithfully is the friend.

We've confused friendship with agreement and love with approval. "Iron sharpens iron," but sharpening grinds and throws sparks. There's a strong case for gentleness: the world is full of critics, people are more fragile than they look, and the church has a long record of cruelty dressed as truth-telling. All of that is true. But the faithful wound differs from the careless one in its motive, the friend's good rather than the speaker's satisfaction. And the reason we don't tell our friends the hard truth is rarely that we're protecting them. Usually we're protecting ourselves, and calling it kindness.

keyScripture.why: "Faithful are the wounds of a friend; profuse are the kisses of an enemy" (Proverbs 27:6). The hard truth spoken in love is called faithful, and endless flattery from someone who won't risk a hard word is called the mark of an enemy. It overturns our instinct that a friend is someone who only ever affirms us.

discussion.q: By the measure that a close friend tells you hard truths, do you have a close friend? When did someone last love you enough to wound you?
discussion.behind: Open with the uncomfortable test, gently. Most people have never measured friendship this way, and the answer often unsettles them. The point isn't to make anyone feel unloved but to show how our friendships have been arranged around comfort. Let the silence after the question do its work.

discussion.q: Read Proverbs 27:5-6. Why does calling the wounding friend faithful and the flatterer an enemy reverse our instincts? Where have you treated the challenging friend as the difficult one and the flatterer as the good one?
discussion.behind: Press on the reversal. We reward the friend who affirms us and quietly resent the one who challenges us, exactly backward from Proverbs. Keep it pointed at ourselves, not at the people we'd like to correct.

discussion.q: "Iron sharpens iron, and one man sharpens another" (Proverbs 27:17). What does it feel like to be sharpened by a friend? Are you in any friendship close enough for that to happen?
discussion.behind: Sharpening involves friction and the wearing away of what shouldn't be there. A friendship with no friction may not be healthy; it may just be too shallow to sharpen anything. Ask whether anyone has avoided that kind of closeness on purpose.

discussion.q: People are fragile and need encouragement more than correction, and the church has done real harm with cruelty dressed as honesty. What's true in that, and where is the line between wounding faithfully and simply wounding?
discussion.behind: Hold both carefully. The caution is real, and no one should leave this session licensed to be harsh. But the line is real too, and it runs through motive, whether the hard word is for the friend's good or the speaker's satisfaction. Read Galatians 6:1 together if it helps.

discussion.q: Where have you called your silence kindness when it was really self-protection?
discussion.behind: Close on ourselves, and go first. We say we withhold the hard truth to spare the friend, but usually we're sparing ourselves the risk. Help the room see that the loving thing and the hard thing are often the same thing. Name your own unspoken word before asking for theirs.

objections.objection: Constantly correcting your friends is exhausting and arrogant. Who made you everyone's judge? People need friends who accept them as they are, not friends who keep pointing out their faults and calling it love.
objections.response: That anger is aimed at something real. Some people mistake a critical spirit for honesty and correct constantly out of a need to feel superior, and being around them is exhausting and wounding. Scripture has no more patience for that than you do. And acceptance is a real gift; the friend who receives you as you are isn't doing something small. Where the objection overshoots is in throwing out the faithful wound along with the careless one, as if the only options were constant criticism or unconditional approval. Proverbs knows a third thing: the rare, costly, well-timed hard truth from someone who has earned the right through years of love, someone who'd rather not say it and says it anyway because your good requires it. The critic wounds often and enjoys it. The friend wounds rarely and hates it.

objections.objection: If a friend really cared about me, they'd support me, not judge my choices. Telling me hard truths I didn't ask for is imposing your opinion on my life, and I get to decide what's right for me.
objections.response: There's a real boundary here worth honoring. No one is owed commentary on every decision; friends aren't each other's managers, and people do get to make their own choices and live with them. But notice the assumption underneath, that support and truthfulness are opposites, that loving someone means affirming whatever they decide. Scripture won't allow that. The friend who watches you walk toward something destructive and says nothing, calling it respect, is offering what Proverbs calls the enemy's kiss, a pleasant silence that costs him nothing and may cost you a great deal. "Better is open rebuke than hidden love" (Proverbs 27:5). You do get to decide. A true friend also gets to tell you when he fears you're wrong, and then keep loving you whichever way you choose.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: What's the hard true thing a good friend would tell you right now if they loved you enough to risk it? Why has no one said it, or have you arranged your life so no one could?
sessions.practice: This week, do the harder of two things. Either receive a hard truth, by asking a trusted friend to tell you a blind spot they've seen and been too kind to name, and then not defending yourself when they do. Or speak one, by going to a friend you've watched walk toward something costly and saying, gently, the true thing you've been swallowing, for their good and not your satisfaction. Write down what you were afraid of, and whether the fear was really for them or for you.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord, you gave us a proverb we don't have the stomach for, that the wounds of a friend are faithful and the kisses of an enemy are many, and we've built friendships that can't survive an honest word. We've called the flatterer a good friend and the truth-teller difficult, kept silent where love required speech, and named our cowardice kindness. Forgive us. Give us friends who love us enough to wound us, and make us those friends, reluctant and truthful and never cruel. Teach us the difference between harshness that serves the speaker and the wound that serves the friend. Let us be sharpened, even where it grinds. Amen.
reflection: When did a friend last tell me a hard truth, and if it's been a long time, have I made myself impossible to tell?
Whom have I pulled close because they affirm me, and whom have I quietly pushed away because they challenge me?
Where have I stayed silent with a friend and called it kindness, when it was really fear protecting my own comfort?
sessions.teaching:
One sure sign that you don't actually have a close friend isn't that you feel lonely at parties. It's that no one has told you a hard truth about yourself in years. That runs against nearly everything our culture trains us to want from friendship. We want friends who make us feel good, take our side, and tell us we're right, and by that standard the best friend is the one who affirms us most reliably. Scripture says almost the reverse. A friend, in the Bible's account, is someone who tells you what's true, especially when it's what you least want to hear: "Faithful are the wounds of a friend; profuse are the kisses of an enemy" (Proverbs 27:6).

Read that slowly, because it turns our instinct over. The one who wounds you, when the wound is faithful, is the friend. The one who covers you in agreement and never risks a hard word, whose kisses are profuse, is acting as an enemy, because the flattery costs him nothing and leaves you unchanged and unwarned. "Better is open rebuke than hidden love" (Proverbs 27:5). Somewhere we confused friendship with agreement and love with approval, until a friend became someone whose job is to validate us.

Scripture's picture isn't gentle. "Iron sharpens iron, and one man sharpens another" (Proverbs 27:17). When iron sharpens iron there's friction and sparks and the grinding away of what's dull and bent until an edge appears. A friendship with no friction at all may not be peaceful. It may just be too shallow to sharpen anything, two blades that never touch.

There's a strong case for gentleness, and I hold much of it myself. The world is already full of critics. People are more fragile and more wounded than they let on, and most need encouragement far more than one more person pointing out their faults. And the church has a long and ugly record here: people who used the language of truth to license contempt, who wounded carelessly, called it love, and left real damage behind. All of that is true. But the argument goes wrong when it throws out the faithful wound with the careless one, as if the only choices were harsh correction or endless approval. Paul shows a third way: "Brothers, if anyone is caught in any transgression, you who are spiritual should restore him in a spirit of gentleness. Keep watch on yourself, lest you too be tempted" (Galatians 6:1). The faithful wound is rare, costly and well timed, and it comes from someone who has earned the right through proven love, who'd rather not say it and says it anyway. The line between wounding faithfully and just wounding runs through motive. Is the hard word for the friend's good or the speaker's satisfaction? Does the person wound reluctantly and rarely, or often and with some pleasure? You can usually feel from the inside which side of that line you're on.

Now the part most of us know from the inside and don't enjoy admitting. The real reason we don't tell our friends the hard truth is almost never that we're protecting them. We say we don't want to hurt them, that it isn't our place, that they're going through enough. But underneath, most of the time, we're protecting ourselves: the comfort of the friendship, our standing in their eyes, the discomfort and risk of the conversation. Most of us have watched a friend walk toward something we feared would cost them, said nothing, and called it kindness. It wasn't. It was fear wearing kindness as a coat. The loving thing and the hard thing are often the same thing, and what separates them is usually our own fear. If you want to know whether you have friends of the first kind, ask when one of them last told you something true that hurt. If you want to know whether you are one, ask whom you've been sparing, and whether you were really sparing them.

scriptureStudy.note: "Faithful are the wounds of a friend; profuse are the kisses of an enemy." The honest wound is called faithfulness and the endless flattery enmity, which makes us ask whether we chose our friends for their truth or only their comfort.
"Iron sharpens iron, and one man sharpens another." Sharpening takes friction. A friendship with no edge may simply be too shallow to sharpen anyone.
"Better is open rebuke than hidden love." Love that feels affection but never risks a hard word is worth less than an honest rebuke.

"Oil and perfume make the heart glad, and the sweetness of a friend comes from his earnest counsel." A friend's sweetness lies not in agreement but in earnest counsel, thinking hard about your good and telling you what he sees.
"Whoever rebukes a man will afterward find more favor than he who flatters with his tongue." The hard word stings first and earns deeper trust in the end.

"You who are spiritual should restore him in a spirit of gentleness. Keep watch on yourself." Truthfulness paired with gentleness and humility, ruling out both the silence that abandons a friend and the harshness that wounds him carelessly.
"Speaking the truth in love, we are to grow up in every way into him who is the head, into Christ." Truth and love are held together, and the aim of the honest word is the friend's growth.

sessions.goingDeeper:
Look at how truthfulness and accountability actually work in friendship, testing what our culture says against what Scripture says. The therapeutic account of relationships tends to prize affirmation and unconditional acceptance above everything, and a group should grant what it gets right: shame-driven criticism is destructive, and many people carry wounds that mean they need to be received before they can be challenged. The order matters, love first and then the hard word from inside the love. But that account, taken alone, has no place for the faithful wound and tends to read every hard truth as an attack on the self, which leaves a person surrounded by affirmation and unprotected from their own blind spots. Proverbs assumes something different, that we can't see ourselves clearly and need another's loving correction, an account of human nature that takes self-deception seriously.

Then look at a practice the church has nearly lost, the mutual accountability of Christian friendship, where believers watched over one another's souls, asked hard questions, confessed sin to one another and were restored. Dietrich Bonhoeffer argued in Life Together that a person left alone with his sin is utterly alone, and that a brother or sister breaks that isolation by hearing the truth and speaking it, so that confession and honest accountability are among friendship's deepest gifts rather than intrusions on it. Ask whether you have any friendship with that kind of permission in it, and whether the loss of such friendships has left many people both more affirmed and more alone.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose a woman in your group is gentle and avoids conflict. She's proud that she's always encouraging and never critical, and when the session names the faithful wound she's troubled, because she has always believed that never saying a hard word was her best quality as a friend.

Her gentleness is a real gift, and in a world full of critics an encouraging friend is precious, so don't treat her kindness as a fault. But a friend who can never say a hard word is also the friend who watches you walk toward a cliff and offers only encouragement on the way. Proverbs would gently call that the "hidden love" worth less than open rebuke. How would you honor her gentleness and still ask her, kindly, whether there's anyone she loves enough to risk their disapproval for their good? How would you help her see the difference between kindness and fear of conflict?

memoryVerse.text: Faithful are the wounds of a friend; profuse are the kisses of an enemy.

sessions.title: I Have Called You Friends
sessions.aim: To sit with what Jesus said the night before he died, that he no longer calls his followers servants but friends, and to see friendship not as a lesser love beneath the divine ones but as the shape of the love God offers, refusing both a distant religion that keeps God only a master and a sentimental one that makes him a buddy.
sessions.summary:
The most striking sentence about friendship in Scripture isn't spoken by a poet or a king. It's spoken by Jesus on the last night of his life, to a room of men about to abandon him: "No longer do I call you servants... but I have called you friends." Everything about the relationship should run the other way. He is Lord; servant would already have been generous. Instead, hours before the cross, he says friend, and he defines it at once: "Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends."

There's a strong case for keeping God at a reverent distance, that calling God our friend shrinks the Almighty to a buddy. The danger is real; a chummy God who exists to affirm us is an idol. But we didn't reach up and claim the friendship. God reached down and named it, from inside the room where he was about to die. Scripture had pointed this way all along: God spoke to Moses "as a man speaks to his friend," Abraham was called "a friend of God," and Jesus was mocked as "a friend of tax collectors and sinners" and wore it as a title.

keyScripture.why: "No longer do I call you servants, for the servant does not know what his master is doing; but I have called you friends, for all that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you" (John 15:15). On the night before the cross Jesus reaches past "servant" to "friend," describing a relationship not of distant command but of a friend who holds nothing back.

discussion.q: On the last night of his life, Jesus told men who were about to abandon him that he called them friends. What astonishes you about that word, at that moment, to those people?
discussion.behind: Start with how strange it is before any doctrine. Everything about the relationship points to "servant," and that would already be gracious. That Jesus reaches past it, hours before the cross, to men he knows will run, is close to scandalous. Help the room hear a phrase they've heard too often to hear.

discussion.q: Read John 15:12-15. Jesus defines friendship right away as laying down your life. How does that compare with what you usually mean by "friend"?
discussion.behind: Press on the gap. We use "friend" for the light and casual. Jesus fills it with the heaviest love there is. Let the size of his meaning show how small ours has become, without scolding anyone for ordinary speech.

discussion.q: Some worry that calling God our friend is presumptuous, shrinking the Almighty into a buddy and losing the fear of the Lord. What's true in that worry, and what would be lost if it silenced the word Jesus actually used?
discussion.behind: Hold both halves. A sentimental God who exists to affirm us is an idol, and reverence matters. But the word wasn't our presumption; it was his gift. Help the room hold reverence and friendship together, refusing both cold distance and cheap familiarity.

discussion.q: The friendship wasn't us reaching up to claim God but God reaching down to name us. How does it change things to know it was his initiative?
discussion.behind: This is the heart of the gospel here. We didn't earn or claim the friendship, and that's the relief. God named it first, at his own cost, toward people who would fail him. The closeness offered is safe because it rests on his faithfulness, not on our performance.

discussion.q: Read Luke 7:34. Jesus was mocked as "a friend of tax collectors and sinners" and wore it as a title. Are you more comfortable being the friend or being befriended? Whom would you rather not befriend?
discussion.behind: Close on the gift and the calling. Jesus befriended exactly the people friendship is usually rationed away from; that's grace toward us and a pattern for us. Go first by naming where you'd rather keep friendship respectable and safe.

objections.objection: Calling God your friend is arrogant and casual. He's the Almighty, and reducing him to a buddy cheapens him and loses the reverence and fear Scripture clearly commands.
objections.response: That concern guards something precious, and Scripture guards it too. The fear of the Lord is real. God is holy and not tame, and a religion that has turned him into an affirming buddy has lost the God of the burning bush and the whirlwind. That danger should be named. Where the objection goes wrong is in charging the wrong party with presumption. We didn't reach up and claim the friendship. Jesus reached down and named it on the night before he died, and a word God chooses for his relationship with us isn't ours to reject as too familiar. The wonder is that the Holy One, without ceasing to be holy, came near enough to call us friends. The right response isn't to correct him toward more distance but to be undone that the God we should fear has offered what we wouldn't have dared ask for. The friend who died for us is the Lord before whom we fall down.

objections.objection: If God is my friend, why does he feel so absent? Real friends come when you need them and answer when you call. A friend you can't see or hear, who lets you suffer, doesn't match anything I mean by friendship.
objections.response: That ache is real and old, and the silence of God in suffering is one of the hardest things a believer carries. No quick answer honors it. But notice what kind of friendship Jesus named. He didn't promise a friend who spares you all pain. He defined friendship as laying down your life for your friends, and then he proved it on a cross. The friendship God offers isn't the absence of suffering but his presence in it, which is harder and deeper than a friend who keeps trouble away. Jonathan crossed into David's wilderness. God crossed into ours, all the way into death. That doesn't make the silence painless, and this study won't pretend it does. But it means the absence you feel isn't abandonment. The friend who seems silent is the one who has already gone into the grave ahead of us.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If Jesus said to you what he said in that room, that he no longer calls you a servant but a friend, could you receive it, or would something in you insist on keeping him at the distance of a master?
sessions.practice: This week, sit with the sentence as though it were spoken to you: "I have called you friends." Notice what rises, relief or resistance or the reflex to keep God at arm's length, and bring that to him in prayer. Then do one thing that reflects his friendship outward. Befriend someone the way he befriended sinners: someone outside your comfortable circle, with nothing to offer you, someone the respectable would overlook. Write down what it stirs in you to be called a friend by God, and where you'd rather keep both his friendship and your own too safe to cost anything.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord Jesus, on the last night of your life, in a room full of men about to abandon you, you reached past the word servant, which would have been mercy enough, and called them friends, and then you went out and proved the word by dying for them. We've made the word small and casual, and we've made you either a distant master or a buddy we no longer revere. Both are ways of refusing the friendship you offered. Forgive us. Teach us to receive it, that the Holy One came near enough to call us friends and laid down his life to make it true. And teach us to befriend as you did, the sinner, the overlooked, the one with nothing to give. Amen.
reflection: Can I actually receive being called God's friend, or do I keep him at the safer distance of a master I serve but am not known by?
How far has my everyday use of the word "friend" drifted from what Jesus meant by it, the love that lays down its life?
Where would I rather keep friendship respectable and safe, and how does the friend of sinners correct that in me?
sessions.teaching:
The most striking sentence about friendship in Scripture isn't in Proverbs or the story of David and Jonathan, and it isn't spoken by a poet or a philosopher. Jesus says it on the last night of his life, in an upper room, to men he knows are hours from abandoning him: "No longer do I call you servants, for the servant does not know what his master is doing; but I have called you friends, for all that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you" (John 15:15). We've heard it so often we've stopped hearing it.

Think about who is speaking and to whom. He is the one they rightly call Teacher and Lord, the one through whom, John has already told us, "all things were made" (John 1:3). They're his followers, and "servant" is the honest word for the relationship. Coming from God, it would have been generous. But Jesus doesn't stop there. Hours before he's arrested, he reaches past the word that would already have been a gift and says "friend." Then, because he knows we'll sentimentalize it, he defines it at once: "Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends" (John 15:13). And in the same breath: "This is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you" (John 15:12). Friendship in the mouth of Jesus isn't the light and optional thing we've made it. It's the heaviest love there is. He's telling these men, on the eve of proving it, that he's about to die for the friends who will run from the garden and deny him by a fire.

There's a serious case for keeping God at a reverent distance, and its pull is real. Calling God your friend, the objection runs, is presumptuous. He's the Almighty, the God of the burning bush who told Moses to take off his sandals, and calling him a buddy shrinks him to our size and trades the God of the whirlwind for a mascot. That danger is real, and much of the modern church has fallen into it, building a chummy, harmless God who is really our own preferences with a halo. That God is an idol, and the reverence the objection protects is right. But the objection aims its charge at us, as if we'd grabbed a familiarity we had no right to. Read the sentence again and notice its direction. The servants didn't announce they were now the Master's friends. The Master reached down, from inside the room where he was about to die, and named them his friends. It's his gift, and a word God himself chooses isn't ours to hand back as too intimate.

Once you see that, hints across Scripture light up. "Thus the LORD used to speak to Moses face to face, as a man speaks to his friend" (Exodus 33:11). Abraham is called God's friend in three different books, and James, recalling that "Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness," adds that "he was called a friend of God" (James 2:23). And Jesus, during his ministry, was sneered at by the respectable: "Look at him! A glutton and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners!" (Luke 7:34). He didn't deny it or soften it. He let the insult stand as a title, because befriending the people friendship is usually rationed away from is exactly the kind of friend he is.

Here's where many of us have to admit our resistance. We're often more comfortable with God as a master we serve than as a friend who knows us, because a master keeps his distance and a friend comes close, and closeness is what the self-protected heart has trained itself to avoid. We can serve God from across the room. Being called his friend asks us to let him near. But the gospel won't leave us at that distance. It isn't mainly that God became our master, though he is our Lord. It's that the Holy One, without laying aside his holiness, came near enough to call us friends, and then walked out of that room and proved the word by laying down his life for the friends who ran.

scriptureStudy.note: "Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends." Jesus defines friendship by the cross before he reaches it.

"You are my friends if you do what I command you... I have called you friends, for all that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you." Friendship with Christ is marked by obedience and by his telling us what he has heard from the Father.
"This is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you." The friendship we receive becomes the love we owe, measured by how he has loved us.
"The LORD used to speak to Moses face to face, as a man speaks to his friend." Long before the upper room, Scripture describes God's dealings with a man in the language of friendship.
"He was called a friend of God." Abraham's title shows the friendship Jesus names runs through the whole story, offered by God and received by faith.
"A friend of tax collectors and sinners!" The respectable meant it as an insult. Jesus wore it as a title.
"Jesus wept." At the tomb of his friend Lazarus, the friend Jesus is enters our loss and weeps in it.

sessions.goingDeeper:
Think through the weight of the word Jesus chose, because the friendship of God isn't a devotional flourish. It changes how we understand the whole relationship. Scripture holds together, without embarrassment, two things we tend to treat as opposites: God's holiness and his friendship, the consuming fire and the one who calls us friends. A group should resist collapsing either into the other, the cold distance that keeps only the majesty or the sentimental religion that keeps only the closeness. The sociologist Christian Smith, studying the faith of American teenagers, named the folk religion he found "moralistic therapeutic deism," a God who exists mainly to help us feel good about ourselves and otherwise stays out of the way. The friendship of God in Scripture is the opposite of that: costly, proven at a cross, and asking everything.

Then turn to what this means for human friendship. If the highest friendship is the one God offers, laying down his life for his friends, then Christian friendship is meant to reflect that self-giving, and the friend of sinners becomes the pattern for how we befriend: the overlooked, the outsider, the person with nothing to give back, the friendship of usefulness turned inside out. Ask too whether a culture that reads every deep love as romance struggles with a Lord who calls his followers friends and weeps at a friend's grave, and whether recovering the friendship of God might help us recover deep, chaste, self-giving human friendship.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose a man in your group is a faithful, disciplined believer who speaks easily about serving God, obeying God and working for God, but grows visibly uncomfortable when the language turns to being befriended by God. Finally he says it feels presumptuous, almost irreverent, and he'd rather keep a proper distance.

His reverence is real and even admirable, and a faith that has lost all reverence is worse off than his, so don't treat his discomfort as hardness. But a man who will only serve God and never be befriended by him may have arranged things so God stays safely across the room. His reverence may also be doing double duty as a hiding place. How would you honor it and still ask him, gently, why he can accept being God's servant but not God's friend? How might the distance he keeps from God connect to the distance he keeps from people?
