sessions.title: Keeping Friendship in a Distracted Age
sessions.aim: To take seriously the practical crisis of friendship, the moving and busyness and screens that starve it, and to recover the ordinary, repeated work of keeping a friend, refusing both the despair that says deep friendship is impossible now and the sentimentality that thinks it costs nothing.
sessions.summary:
After four sessions on what friendship is, someone always asks the practical question: in a life this full and this scattered, how does anyone actually keep a friend? The trouble isn't that we don't value friendship. It's that modern life quietly starves it, because friendship, unlike marriage or family, has almost no structures left to hold it. We move for work, we're exhausted by evening, and the screen offers an easy imitation of connection that feels like friendship and slowly replaces it, a "like" where a visit used to be.

Augustine knew how deep friendship can go. In the Confessions he describes a friend's death that so undid him that his hometown became a torment, and he says he had loved a mortal as though he would never die. Keeping a friend costs what our age has least of, time and presence. Some loneliness really is structural, and realism about that is right. But realism isn't surrender. The friendships that last in a scattered age aren't the lucky ones. They're the ones somebody decided to keep, on purpose, against the drift.

keyScripture.why: "And let us consider how to stir up one another to love and good works, not neglecting to meet together, as is the habit of some, but encouraging one another" (Hebrews 10:24-25). Meeting together is a habit to be guarded on purpose, and the warning names exactly what a distracted age lets lapse.

discussion.q: Friendship, unlike marriage or family, has almost no structures left to hold it. What used to hold your friendships together, and which of those have you lost?
discussion.behind: Start with the diagnosis. Friendship once rode on nearness, the neighborhood, the church, the settled town, and most of us have lost those without replacing them. Help the room see that the thinning isn't only a failure of will but the loss of the scaffolding friendship leaned on. Name the structural before the personal.

discussion.q: Augustine said that when his friend died it felt as though half his own soul had died, and that he had loved a mortal as though he'd never die. What does that grief tell you about how deeply he'd let himself love a friend?
discussion.behind: His grief was only possible because he had let a friend all the way in, the opposite of our carefully managed friendships. Let the room feel both the beauty and the risk of loving a friend that deeply.

discussion.q: Where has the screen's easy imitation of connection quietly replaced the real thing in your friendships?
discussion.behind: Press gently, without a lecture on technology. Screens aren't evil; they're convincing, offering just enough connection to quiet the hunger without feeding it. Help people notice where a comment or a like has come to stand in for presence, and where a friendship has lapsed without anyone deciding to end it.

discussion.q: Some loneliness is structural; you can't will yourself back into the villages of the past. What's true in that, and where does realism turn into surrender?
discussion.behind: Hold both. The realism is right; shaming people for structural loneliness is cruel and false. But realism becomes surrender the moment it stops being an explanation and starts being an excuse.

discussion.q: Friendship in this age won't happen by accident. What's one deliberate, costly, ordinary thing you could do to keep a friendship against the drift, and what has stopped you?
discussion.behind: Close on the concrete act. The whole study lands here, in the returned call, the guarded evening, the visit that costs something. Help people move from agreeing that friendship matters to naming one thing they'll do. Go first, and name the excuse you've used.

objections.objection: This is just nostalgia. The world has changed, people move for jobs, everyone's busy, and you can't recreate the small towns of the past. Pining for some lost age of deep friendship is unrealistic.
objections.response: Most of that is simply true. The structures that once held friendship have dissolved, people move for work and are pressed for time, and there's no going back to a village that no longer exists. Nostalgia that only mourns and does nothing is self-indulgent, and shaming people for a loneliness the shape of their lives produced is cruel. Where the objection slides is in moving from "this is hard" to "therefore nothing can be done." Those aren't the same claim. Friendships do survive in a scattered age, and they aren't the product of better luck. They come from someone deciding to return the call, guard the evening, book the flight and refuse to let it lapse. Realism about the difficulty is truthful. Using the difficulty to excuse giving up is resignation, and it leaves you exactly as alone as the age would have you.

objections.objection: I keep up with my friends online. I see their lives, I comment, I stay in touch across any distance. That's friendship adapted to the modern world, not a lesser substitute. Insisting on in-person presence is refusing to accept how connection works now.
objections.response: There's real good in that. Staying in contact across distance matters; a friend across the country you can still reach is better than one you've lost, and these tools have kept alive friendships that geography once would have ended. But there's a difference between contact and presence, and our age depends on our confusing them. Seeing a friend's life on a screen isn't the same as being in it, and the imitation is dangerous because it's convincing, offering just enough connection to quiet the hunger while never feeding it. Augustine didn't grieve a man he'd commented on. He grieved a man whose life was bound up with his, and that kind of bond is built by presence, by time and shared rooms. Use the tools gladly to keep a distant friend within reach. Just don't let the tool convince you it's the friendship.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: Which friendship is dying right now not from any rupture but simply from drift, and what deliberate thing would it take to keep it that you haven't been willing to do?
sessions.practice: This week, pick the one friendship most worth keeping and do the deliberate, costly, ordinary thing to keep it. Return the call you've been meaning to return. Guard an evening and give it to a friend in person. Book the visit that costs a plane ticket. Put a standing time on the calendar that recurs whether you feel like it or not, a small structure to hold what our age leaves unstructured. Notice, too, how much of your sense of connection has quietly become the screen's imitation. Write down the friendship you're choosing to keep on purpose, and the drift you're choosing to fight.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, you made us for each other and said it wasn't good to be alone, and then we built a world that scatters us across cities and screens and calls the loneliness inevitable. We've let good friendships die of nothing worse than drift, traded presence for a like, and used the real difficulty of our time as an excuse to do nothing. Forgive us the friends we lost without ever deciding to lose them. Give us resolve to keep friendship on purpose, against the current, with the plain tools of the returned call, the guarded evening and the costly visit. Teach us to love a friend deeply enough that losing one would grieve us as Augustine grieved. Make us people who do the ordinary, faithful work of not being alone, and who help others out of their loneliness too. Amen.
reflection: Which friendships have I lost not to conflict but to drift, and what would it have cost to keep them?
Where has the screen's imitation quietly replaced real presence in my friendships, leaving me feeling connected while actually alone?
What deliberate, recurring practice could I build to keep a friendship against the current of a life that scatters it?
sessions.teaching:
After four sessions on what friendship is, someone always asks the question that keeps people up at night, and it isn't a theological one. It's practical. Granting all of that, how does anyone keep a friend in a life this full and this scattered? That question deserves an answer rather than a sermon, because the crisis of friendship in our time isn't mainly that we've stopped valuing it. Ask people and they'll say friendship matters enormously. The crisis is that the shape of modern life quietly starves it, and in a way that's hard to see, because friendship has almost no structures left to hold it.

Think about it. Romance has marriage, dating, set-aside evenings, a whole culture that makes room for it. Family has the household, the holidays, the obligation of blood that's there whether you tend it or not. Friendship has no vow, no ceremony, no household, no slot on the calendar the culture reserves for it. It survives on whatever margin is left over, and modern life leaves almost none. We move for work, so the friend who knew us is three cities away. We're worn out at the end of the day, so the evening goes to the couch. And the screen does the subtlest thing of all. It offers an imitation of connection that feels enough like friendship to quiet the hunger, a like where a visit used to be, a comment where a conversation used to be, so we can watch a friend's life scroll past and feel we're keeping up while the friendship quietly dies. Nobody decides to end it; it just fades.

The ache isn't new, even if its causes are. Augustine, writing his Confessions at the end of the fourth century, describes the death of a close friend from his youth, and it's one of the most searching accounts of grief ever written. He says the loss so undid him that his hometown became a torment, that everywhere he looked he expected to see his friend, and that he had become a great question to himself. He felt that half his soul had died with the man. Looking back, he says he had poured out his soul on the sand by loving a mortal as though he would never die. His grief was terrible because the friendship had been real, held nothing back, and lacked the careful self-protection that governs so many of our friendships. Often our griefs are smaller because our friendships are.

So what does it cost to keep a friend? Scripture gives an uncomfortable answer: time and presence, the two things our age has least of and guards most closely. Paul wrote to the Thessalonians, "we were ready to share with you not only the gospel of God but also our own selves, because you had become very dear to us" (1 Thessalonians 2:8). John, who could have kept writing letters, said, "I hope to see you soon, and we will talk face to face" (3 John 14). There's no shortcut and no app for it.

There's a strong case for realism, and I hold most of it. Circumstances really have changed. You can't will yourself back into a settled village where friendship rode along on nearness. Some of the loneliness of our time is structural, built into how we work and move, and it isn't fair or true to lay it all on individual failure. But there's a line realism shouldn't cross, where truthfulness about difficulty becomes resignation dressed up as wisdom. "This is hard" is true. "Therefore nothing can be done" isn't. Lasting friendships do exist in this scattered age, and when you look closely they're never simply the lucky ones. They're the ones somebody decided to keep, using tools so plain they're almost embarrassing to name: the returned phone call, the evening guarded and given away in person, the visit that costs a plane ticket and a day off, the standing time on the calendar that recurs whether anyone feels like it, a small structure built to hold what the culture no longer holds for us. "Let us consider how to stir up one another to love and good works, not neglecting to meet together, as is the habit of some" (Hebrews 10:24-25). It isn't a secret; it's work, ordinary and repeated.

Most of us, and I'm one of them, have failed at this more than we've succeeded. We've let good friendships die of nothing more dramatic than drift, told ourselves we'd reconnect when things slowed down, and things never slowed down. So I'm not preaching down at anyone. I'm naming a fight we keep losing. And I won't tie a bow on it. Nothing about this age favors friendship. It will happen on purpose, at some cost, against the current, or it won't happen. The God who looked at a man with everything and said it wasn't good for him to be alone is still asking whether we'll do the ordinary, costly work of not being alone, and whether we'll help the people around us out of their loneliness too.

scriptureStudy.note: "Let us consider how to stir up one another... not neglecting to meet together, as is the habit of some." Meeting together is a habit to guard on purpose, and some were already letting it lapse.
"Better is a neighbor who is near than a brother who is far away." Scripture prizes the friend who is near and present, the very nearness a mobile age makes hard to keep.
"Rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep." Friendship is shared joy and shared grief, which takes being there.
"Bear one another's burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ." Friendship in Scripture isn't easy contact but carrying another's weight, which takes presence, time and cost.
"We were ready to share with you not only the gospel of God but also our own selves." True friendship shares the self, not only news about the self.
"I hope to see you soon, and we will talk face to face." Even an apostle who could write a letter wanted to be there in person. The letter, like the screen, is a gift and not a substitute.
"If two lie together, they keep warm, but how can one keep warm alone?" The image is bodily and near, a warmth the isolated life can't make on its own.

sessions.goingDeeper:
Look at the structural forces this session names, because understanding the water we swim in is part of learning to swim against it. Robert Putnam's Bowling Alone documented the decline across the second half of the twentieth century of the clubs, leagues, lodges and civic groups through which ordinary friendship once formed almost on its own. Grant the strength of his account: the thinning is real, measured and consequential, not a matter of individual laziness. The Surgeon General's 2023 advisory points the same way, describing fewer close friendships, more time alone, and real effects on health. Take those findings at their strongest, then bring them under Scripture rather than beside it. They describe the symptom accurately. They can't supply the cure, which is a people willing to build, on purpose and at cost, the fellowship the culture no longer builds for them.

This is where the local church has a strange and underused gift. It's one of the few institutions left that gathers the same people in the same place at the same time, week after week, across age and class and season of life, which is exactly the soil friendship needs. Ask whether you've treated the church as a service to attend or a people to belong to, and whether the deliberate friendship this study describes might find in an ordinary congregation the structure that marriage and family have and friendship lost. Augustine's grief, David's lament and Jesus weeping at a friend's tomb all say that friendship is worth the cost of loving what you can lose.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose a woman in your group says near the end of the study that all of this is a little painful. She has moved three times in ten years for her husband's work and has no deep friendships where she lives now. She feels the study has named a wound without giving her any realistic way to heal it, since she can't create years of shared history overnight. She isn't being difficult; she's describing a hard situation.

Her situation is hard, the moves aren't her fault, and deep friendship does take time she hasn't yet had there, so don't hand her a cheerful formula. But listen for the quiet despair in "nothing can be done," and gently separate it from "it can't happen instantly." Every deep friendship that exists began as a first deliberate step by someone who didn't have it yet. How would you honor her grief for the friendships the moves cost her, and still help her see that the friendships she'll have where she lives now are the ones she begins? How could this group be part of where that begins?

leaderPrimer:
The particular danger of a study on friendship is that it opens a wound most people have learned to keep covered. Nearly everyone in your room is lonelier than they'll admit on the first night, and some carry it as a private shame, a suspicion that if they have fewer friends than they should, something must be wrong with them. So set the tone the first night and keep it every night after. The loneliness of our time isn't mainly a personal defect. It's the fruit of a whole way of living that starves the very love it now aches for, and no one in the room is on trial for being lonely.

Don't let the group become a place where the socially confident display their full calendars to the isolated. Some of the truest movement in these sessions, the friendship let slip into acquaintance, the hard word never spoken, the God kept at a master's distance, the friend lost to drift, will happen in silence, between a person and God. Make room for that silence rather than demanding confession around the circle.

One more thing, and it isn't optional. In almost any group there's someone whose loneliness has become real isolation, someone for whom this study touches real pain, grief, depression, the ache of a person who truly has no one. Watch for them. Be available privately. Know the resources in your church and community, and where someone's isolation shades into something darker, do not try to be their only friend and their counselor both, but help them toward real help while genuinely befriending them yourself.

Lead from inside this, not above it. The study names the common failures at friendship plainly, the calls not returned, the brothers let slip into contacts, and it asks you to name your own. If you present yourself as the person with the rich, full circle speaking down to the lonely, the room will perform for you and nothing will move. Go in as someone living in the same starved age, still learning the deliberate work you're asking of them. Five weeks won't hand anyone the friendships they lack. It can name the love we forgot and send people home determined to do the ordinary, costly work of not being alone, and perhaps a little more willing to begin it with each other.

faq.q: Is this study just going to make lonely people feel worse about being lonely?
faq.a: No, and it works against exactly that. The first session insists that the loneliness of our time isn't mainly a personal defect but the fruit of a way of living that starves the love it aches for, so no one is on trial for being lonely. The study names the ache truthfully, but as something the culture produced, not something the lonely person failed at, and it points toward a real if costly way forward. The last session is entirely practical. It refuses both the despair that says deep friendship is impossible now and the sentimentality that thinks it costs nothing, and it lands on ordinary work anyone can begin, often with the very group they studied it in.

faq.q: What if someone in the group is genuinely isolated and this study touches real pain?
faq.a: Take it with complete seriousness, because in almost any group there's someone whose loneliness has become real isolation, and the study is built to make room for that. The leader primer asks leaders to watch for that person, be available privately, and know the resources in their church and community before they begin. Where someone's isolation shades into grief, depression, or something darker, the leader is urged not to try to be that person's only friend and counselor both, but to help them toward real help while genuinely befriending them. The study takes the pain seriously without agreeing with despair, and it insists that the answer to isolation isn't more self-sufficiency but the slow work of being known, begun somewhere safe. If anyone is in crisis, connect them to real help and do not leave them to carry it alone.

faq.q: Is this going to be an awkward study where we're all made to confess how few friends we have?
faq.a: No. The leader primer says plainly that much of the truest work will happen in silence, between a person and God, and that the leader should make room for that silence rather than demanding confession around the circle. No one has to announce their loneliness or perform their social life. The questions can be answered as openly or as privately as each person is ready for, and every session ends in prayer rather than an uncomfortable accounting. The aim is a room safe enough for people to be candid if they choose, never one that pries. What's said in the room stays in the room, and no one is put on the spot.

faq.q: What's the difference between the three kinds of friendship the study keeps mentioning?
faq.a: The distinction comes from Aristotle, and it still holds. There's the friendship of usefulness, kept because the other person can do something for you. There's the friendship of pleasure, kept because the other person is good company. Both are real and neither is evil, but both last only as long as the usefulness or the fun lasts, because what you loved was what the person gave you. And there's the friendship of two people who want each other's good and are made better by knowing each other, which Aristotle called the friendship of virtue, the only kind that lasts when the usefulness dries up and the fun goes quiet. The study uses this to help people see, without shame, how few of their friendships are of the third kind, and to ask what it would cost to build even one.

faq.q: Isn't calling God our friend a bit irreverent, treating the Almighty like a buddy?
faq.a: The study takes that worry seriously, because it guards something precious. A sentimental God who exists to affirm us is an idol, and the fear of the Lord is real and right. But the fourth session makes a crucial point. We didn't reach up and claim the friendship. Jesus reached down and named it, the night before he died: "No longer do I call you servants... but I have called you friends." A word God himself chooses for his relationship with us isn't ours to reject as too familiar. The study refuses both the cold distance that keeps God only a master and the cheap familiarity that makes him a mascot, and holds together what Scripture holds together: God is holy and not tame, and the Holy One came near enough to call us friends and proved it by dying for us.

faq.q: Does the study deal with the loneliness that comes with phones and social media?
faq.a: Yes, carefully, and without a lecture that technology is evil. The final session names the danger precisely: the screen offers an imitation of connection that feels enough like friendship to quiet the hunger while never feeding it, a "like" where a visit used to be. The point isn't that digital tools are wicked but that they're convincing, and that our age depends on our confusing contact with presence. The study grants that staying in touch across distance is a real good. What it refuses is letting the tool convince us it's the friendship, because that leaves a person with a hundred connections and no one to call in the worst hour.

faq.q: The study talks about a friend telling you hard truths. Isn't that just a license to go criticize people?
faq.a: No, and the third session guards against exactly that. It grants that some people mistake a critical spirit for honesty and that the church has done real harm with cruelty dressed as truth-telling, and it says plainly that no one should leave licensed to be harsh. The faithful wound Proverbs describes isn't the critic's reflex. It's rare, costly and well timed, spoken by someone who has earned the right through years of love and would rather not say it. The line runs through motive, whether the hard word is for the friend's good or the speaker's satisfaction. The session actually presses harder on the more common failure, not too much honesty but too little, the silence we call kindness when it's really our own fear.

faq.q: Why does the study spend a whole session on David and Jonathan?
faq.a: Because it's the clearest picture in Scripture of a friendship that rises to the weight of covenant, and it corrects our thinned-out idea of the word. Jonathan was heir to the throne and David was chosen to take it, and Jonathan loved him anyway, made a covenant with him in the LORD's name, gave him his royal robe, warned him against his own father, and strengthened his hand in God in the wilderness at risk to his own life. That isn't a strategic alliance, because everything Jonathan does runs against his own advantage. It shows that friendship can be a bond you promise and not only a mood you feel, and that the binding is what lets it survive strain. When David grieved that Jonathan's love was extraordinary, he had a category for a friendship worth weeping over that we've largely lost.

faq.q: How do I lead this if I'm lonely myself and don't feel qualified to teach about friendship?
faq.a: That isn't a disqualification. It may be your best qualification. The study was written to be led by ordinary people, not the socially gifted, and every question carries notes on what's behind it. The real qualification isn't a full circle of friends but a willingness to be candid about your own loneliness and your own failures at friendship, the calls not returned, the friends let slip into contacts. If you walk in as the person who has friendship figured out, you'll lead from above the room and nothing will move. Your own struggle lets you stand alongside everyone else, and a leader willing to take the first deliberate step toward friendship right there in the group may find the group becomes where their own loneliness begins to lift.

faq.q: Why does the study keep naming the writer's and the leader's own failures instead of just teaching the lesson?
faq.a: Because that's the method. The study names the common failures at friendship plainly, friendships let die from drift, the couch chosen over the call, brothers who became contacts, without exempting the writer or the leader. It isn't false modesty. You can't call people out of a loneliness you pretend to be above, and a study that diagnosed everyone else's isolation from a position of ease would only add shame to the wound. Keeping the writer and the leader inside the struggle makes it safe for the people in the room to be truthful, which is where friendships begin to change.

faq.q: I'm a skeptic. Isn't this just the church trying to boost attendance by telling people they need community?
faq.a: It's a fair suspicion, and the study tries to earn the right to answer it by refusing that move. It doesn't treat friendship as a recruitment tool. It takes the secular research seriously on its own terms first, the Surgeon General's advisory on loneliness and Robert Putnam's account of the decline of associational life, before saying anything religious. What it offers is a particular claim: that the human need to be known and not alone is real, that it was named at the beginning by the God who said it isn't good for the human to be alone, and that friendship at its deepest is a love the modern world lost and would do well to recover. You don't have to share the faith to notice that a civilization measuring loneliness as a health risk might be missing something the ancients and the Scriptures took seriously.

faq.q: Does taking friendship this seriously look down on people who are introverted or private?
faq.a: No, and the study is careful here. It isn't arguing that everyone needs a large circle or a busy social life. The friendship it honors most is about depth, not volume, a single true friend rather than a crowd of contacts, and an introvert with one or two deep, faithful friendships is closer to what Scripture prizes than an extrovert with a hundred shallow ones. It also grants that some seasons and temperaments have less social capacity, and it won't shame anyone for that. What it presses on isn't sociability but isolation, being unknown by anyone, which is different from being quiet or private. The point is that no one, of any temperament, should be left with a life of contacts and no one who truly knows them.

timeline.event: Genesis 2 grounds the need for companionship in creation itself. God looks at a man who has everything and names the one thing not good, that he should be alone, so needing another is part of being human before anything has gone wrong.

The covenant friendship of David and Jonathan is forged in Saul's court, a friendship in which Jonathan's soul is "knit to the soul of David," sealed by an oath in the LORD's name, and mourned by David as a love surpassing the love of women.

Aristotle gives two books of the Nicomachean Ethics to friendship, distinguishing the friendships of usefulness and pleasure from the rare friendship of virtue and ranking true friendship among the highest human goods.
Cicero writes Laelius, On Friendship near the end of his life, treating friendship as among the noblest things in human life and shaping how the West would think about it for centuries.

On the night before his death, Jesus tells his disciples he no longer calls them servants but friends, defines friendship as laying down one's life for one's friends, and then goes to the cross for the friends who abandon him.

Augustine, in the Confessions, describes the death of a friend of his youth and a grief so deep that his hometown became a torment, one of the church's most searching accounts of how closely a friendship can bind two lives.
Aelred of Rievaulx, a Cistercian abbot, writes Spiritual Friendship, drawing on Cicero and arguing that true friendship is not a distraction from the love of God but a school for it.
C. S. Lewis publishes The Four Loves, observing that the ancients counted friendship among the highest human goods while the modern world largely ignores it.
Robert Putnam publishes Bowling Alone, documenting the decline across the second half of the twentieth century of the associational life through which ordinary friendship once formed.

The U.S. Surgeon General issues an advisory, Our Epidemic of Loneliness and Isolation, comparing the health risk of social disconnection to smoking, putting a measurement on a need Genesis named at the beginning.

facilitatorScript.open: Welcome, and thank you for being here. It takes some courage to talk about friendship and loneliness in a room of people. Before we start, three things. First, no one here is on trial for being lonely. The loneliness of our time is largely the fruit of a whole way of living that starves the very love it aches for, so we're here to be truthful, not to be judged, and not to compare whose calendar is fuller. Second, you don't have to perform a rich social life or confess a thin one. You can be private, you can be unsure, and what's said here stays in this room. Third, I'm inside this too, still learning the work this study asks of all of us. We aren't talking about loneliness from a safe distance. One more thing that matters, and I mean it. If anyone here is carrying real isolation, real grief, a loneliness that has become heavy, I am available to talk privately, and you are not alone in this room tonight. Let me read tonight's key passage, and then we'll sit with it before anyone says anything. There are no wrong answers in the first five minutes, only truthful ones.
facilitatorScript.transition: We've looked hard at what this session says. Now let's bring it home, off the page and into the friendships each of us has and doesn't have, because none of this matters if it stays an idea about friendship in general rather than about people whose names we could say right now.
facilitatorScript.close: We're going to stop there, even though it isn't resolved, because loneliness isn't solved in an evening and this study won't pretend it is. Take the weight of this home rather than leaving it at the door. Try the practice this week in one actual friendship, even imperfectly, and sit with the reflection questions on your own. Come back ready to be truthful, not finished. Let me pray for us before we go, and then I'll see you next time, and remember, my door is open if any of you needs it, and this room can be a place a friendship actually begins.

Week 3: Session 2, Souls Knit Together, with extra time on the covenant of David and Jonathan and the cost of Jonathan's love.

Aristotle's term for a bond kept because the other person is good company. Also real, but it dissolves when the enjoyment runs out.

Aristotle's term for the rare, slow bond between two people who want each other's good and are made better by knowing each other. The only kind that lasts when usefulness and pleasure run dry, because it rests on the person.

A friendship that rises to a sworn, faithful commitment rather than a mood that lasts while it lasts, modeled on David and Jonathan, who made a covenant sealed by oath. A chosen faithfulness that says, "I won't let this drift."

The Proverbs image for how friends improve one another, through friction and the grinding away of what's dull and bent. A friendship with no edge may simply be too shallow to sharpen anyone.

promoKit.bulletinBlurb: We have more contacts than any people in history and fewer friends than we can admit, and almost nobody stops to ask what happened to friendship. This five-session study treats friendship the way Scripture does, as a love weighty enough to knit two souls, faithful enough to wound, and costly enough that the Son of God laid down his life for his friends and then called us that. It covers the loneliness of our time, the covenant of David and Jonathan, the friend who tells the hard truth, the friendship Jesus offered the night before he died, and the ordinary work of keeping a friend in a mobile, distracted world. It's frank about the ache and gentle with the lonely. Anyone can lead it. Come as you are, not finished.
